assessment.name: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Child Self Report (ChOCI-R-S)
assessment.description: The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) is a 38-item self-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by the child or adolescent and measures both the obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours they experience and the impairment these cause in daily life. There is also a parent-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-P ) that can be completed by a parent or caregiver.

administration.instructions: Each of the following questions asks you about things or “habits” you feel you have to do although you may know that they do not make sense. Sometimes, you may try to stop from doing them but this might not be possible. You might feel worried or angry or frustrated until you have finished what you have to do. An example of a habit like this may be the need to wash your hands over and over again even though they are not really dirty, or the need to count up to a special number (e.g. 6 or 10) while you do certain things. Please answer each question by indicating how much you agree with the statement, or how much you think it is true of you. Please answer each item, without spending too much time on any one item. There are no right or wrong answers. Compulsions· symptoms

source_rule_excerpts: Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from 0 to 40) Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items

Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range from 0 to 48) Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items

Each raw score is presented with a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample. A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of young people with OCD in the reference group. Because the norms come from an OCD-diagnosed sample, a low percentile does not mean a young person does not have OCD, only that their symptoms or impairment are milder than most others with the condition.

On first administration, the report presents a results table followed by two construct sections (Symptoms and Impairment). Each section contains two horizontal raw-score charts. The first plots the construct’s total as a single bar with the client’s raw score on a 0–40 axis for Symptoms or 0–48 for Impairment. A clinical 25th-to-75th percentile reference rectangle and a dashed line at the clinical average show the score relative to the clinical reference sample of young people with OCD. The second plots the construct’s two subscales (Compulsion and Obsession bars on a 0–20 axis for Symptoms or 0–24 for Impairment, each with its own 25th-to-75th reference rectangle and clinical-average line). Beneath each bar, a coloured strip marks that scale’s descriptor bands (Low, Moderate and High for Symptoms; Minimal, Mild, Moderate, Severe and Extreme for Impairment, with Minimal shown in white).

Reference percentiles are derived from Uher and colleagues (2008): 285 consecutive referrals (244 to 278 with complete self-report data per subscale) to an OCD clinic between 2000 and 2006, all meeting ICD-10 criteria for OCD via structured clinical interview, with no significant sex differences (boys’ age M = 13.7, range 7 to 18; girls’ age M = 13.7, range 9 to 18). Reference parameters for the self-report subscales are: Compulsion Symptoms M = 9.5, SD = 4.3; Obsession Symptoms M = 8.0, SD = 5.1; Total Symptoms M = 17.6, SD = 7.8; Compulsion Impairment M = 15.0, SD = 4.5; Obsession Impairment M = 13.5, SD = 5.2; Total Impairment M = 28.5, SD = 8.7. Because this reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed reference group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a young person diagnosed with OCD, not the general population. No community-sample reference data exists for the self-report ChOCI-R-S, and the original authors note that confirmation in primary care and population-based samples remains needed (Uher et al., 2008).

The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. NovoPsych placed each subscale’s cut-offs at the same percentile as the matching Total cut-off, using each subscale’s own mean and SD from Uher et al. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 16th percentile and High at about the 84th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 56th and Extreme about the 90th. The parent-report ChOCI-R-P has different raw-score cut-offs, because each form is converted through its own column of the equivalence table and its own norms, so the same raw score does not mean the same thing on the two forms.

source_guidance.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Scoring
source_guidance.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The ChOCI-R-S measures both symptoms and impairment:
Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from 0 to 40) Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items
Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range from 0 to 48) Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items
Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the young person to describe their three most upsetting habits (compulsions) and thoughts (obsessions), respectively. These items are not included in the scoring, but provide additional clinical information to inform assessment and treatment planning.

source_guidance.title: ChOCI-R-S Percentiles
source_guidance.text: Each raw score is presented with a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample. A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of young people with OCD in the reference group. Because the norms come from an OCD-diagnosed sample, a low percentile does not mean a young person does not have OCD, only that their symptoms or impairment are milder than most others with the condition.

source_guidance.title: Subscale interpretation of the ChOCI-R-S
source_guidance.text: Each ChOCI-R-S subscale assesses a different aspect of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or associated impairment. Higher scores on Compulsion Symptoms indicate that the young person reports more frequent or more severe compulsive behaviours, such as washing, checking, ordering, counting and reassurance-seeking. Higher scores on Obsession Symptoms indicate more frequent intrusive thoughts of harm, doubt, death, religious or blasphemous content, or aggressive or immoral content. Higher scores on Compulsion Impairment indicate greater functional disruption from compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friends, distress when prevented from acting, difficulty resisting or controlling compulsions, and avoidance. Higher scores on Obsession Impairment indicate similar impacts associated with obsessive thoughts.

source_guidance.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
source_guidance.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations can be evaluated using a Reliable Change Index (RCI). A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment, or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms, indicates a change that is unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone.

source_guidance.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
source_guidance.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations is interpreted via a Reliable Change Index (RCI) computed with the Jacobson-Truax formula, using the Uher and colleagues (2008) self-report internal consistency reliability and standard deviation for each total. A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment (alpha = .86, SD = 8.7), or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms (alpha = .84, SD = 7.8), exceeds measurement error at the 95% confidence level and is interpreted as a reliable change.

source_guidance.title: How should I interpret a large gap between the child-rated ChOCI-R-S and the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P?
source_guidance.text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

source_guidance.title: How should I respond clinically when a young person with elevated ChOCI-R-S scores also presents with anxiety, tics, or attentional difficulties?
source_guidance.text: Co-occurring psychiatric conditions are common in paediatric OCD rather than the exception, with around 74 percent of children meeting criteria for at least one additional disorder (Stiede et al., 2024). Practically, an elevated ChOCI-R-S should prompt considerations of assessment for generalised anxiety, separation anxiety, specific phobias, tic disorders, and ADHD as clinically indicated before finalising a treatment plan. Comorbidity influences sequencing: co-occurring anxiety may require adaptations to treatment planning, tic disorders can blur the line between compulsions and motor/vocal tics on the Compulsion subscale (worth clarifying in interview), and untreated ADHD can undermine engagement with between-session exposure tasks. Documenting which conditions are present, which are driving impairment, and which are likely to interact with CBT-with-ERP is more useful than ChOCI-R-S scores alone.

source_guidance.title: Does a low score or a "Minimal" descriptor mean the young person does not have OCD?
source_guidance.text: No. Because the reference sample was made up entirely of young people diagnosed with OCD, scores describe severity relative to that group rather than to the general population. A low percentile or a “Minimal” descriptor therefore means the young person’s reported symptoms or impairment are lower than those of most young people in the OCD clinical reference sample. The measure should not be used to rule OCD in or out.

source_guidance.title: With six scores produced, which should be the main focus for reporting and progress monitoring?
source_guidance.text: Total Impairment is the primary score for most purposes. It reflects overall OCD-related functional disruption and is comparable to the total score of the clinician-administered CY-BOCS, which makes it a useful headline figure and a key metric for tracking progress over the course of treatment. Total Symptoms complements it by capturing the breadth of symptoms endorsed, while the four subscale scores are best used to examine the balance of obsessions and compulsions and identify domain-specific patterns that may be obscured by the total scores.
